description: AURA-Flux is an open-source, physics-informed geospatial engine for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. By coupling NASA EMIT hyperspectral methane imagery with GEOS-FP wind reanalysis, AURA-Flux automatically transforms static orbital concentration maps into quantified, facility-attributed mass emission rates (kg/hr) with dynamic uncertainty bounds. Our pipeline bridges spaceborne remote sensing and ground-level action to tackle anthropogenic super-emitters in real time
summary: Satellites in space take pictures of invisible greenhouse gas leaks, like methane escaping from factories, but the maps just look like confusing neon ink blots. We built AURA-Flux to solve this. It acts as an "Earth Information Jukebox" by taking NASA satellite images and weather wind data to do two things: first, it calculates the exact gas leak rate in kilograms per hour; second, it turns the data into real musical sounds so blind and low-vision users can hear the size and shape of the gas cloud. It makes NASA open science musical, accessible, and easy for everyone.
details: What it does and how it works: AURA-Flux is a web application that bridges climate science, math, and audio accessibility. It takes NASA satellite measurements and weather wind speeds, runs a physical mass-balance calculation (Integrated Mass Enhancement), and translates the results into both a clean dashboard metric and an interactive web audio tone. Benefits and Intended Impact: The app helps facility operators and regulators quickly find and measure greenhouse gas leaks to stop climate change. It also creates a brand new way for blind or low-vision users to explore satellite climate data through sound. Tools and Languages Used: - Python (for data processing and calculations) - Streamlit (for building the live web app dashboard) - HTML5 Web Audio API (for real-time sound sonification) - GitHub (for open-source code hosting) Why it is creative: Instead of showing boring spreadsheets or confusing scientific charts, AURA-Flux turns invisible environmental gases into music and sound, making climate data truly open and inclusive for everyone.
